title: 03. Databases & Data Modeling: Key-Value Stores
summary: A key-value store is the simplest NoSQL data model — the database is conceptually a giant hash map where every record is addressed by an opaque key and stored as an opaque blob value, giving O(1) get/put complexity,…
objectives: Why is a key-value store O(1), and what does that imply for query flexibility?
What's the difference between Memcached, Redis, and DynamoDB, and when do you choose each?
Explain the cache-aside pattern and its pitfalls (cache stampede, thundering herd).
How does Redis achieve atomicity with single-threading, and what are the trade-offs?

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** A **key-value store** is the simplest NoSQL data model — the database is conceptually a giant **hash map** where every record is addressed by an opaque key and stored as an opaque blob value, giving **O(1) `get`/`put`** complexity, sub-millisecond latency, and trivial horizontal partitioning (hash the key), exemplified by **Redis** (in-memory data structures), **Memcached** (pure cache), and **Amazon DynamoDB** (managed, durable, scaled), and used for **caching, session storage, leaderboards, real-time bidding, and rate limiting** where the access pattern is always "I know the exact key, give me its value."

Key-value stores occupy the simplest corner of the NoSQL landscape: there are no tables, no joins, no query language (beyond key lookup), and no schema — just `GET key`, `SET key value`, `DELETE key`. This radical simplicity is the source of their power. The data model is a hash map, and hash maps are O(1) — which means a single Redis instance can serve 100k+ operations per second on a single core, and DynamoDB can serve any scale transparently because the underlying operation is trivially partitionable (hash the key, route to the owning shard). The trade-off is equally radical: if your access pattern is anything other than "I have the exact key, give me the value," key-value stores are the wrong tool. Want to query "all users older than 30"? You need a secondary index (which DynamoDB charges for, Redis doesn't natively have). Want to atomically update two keys? You need transactions (Redis has `MULTI/EXEC` for same-instance, DynamoDB has transactions across items in same or different tables). Want joins? Not happening — denormalize at write time. The key-value philosophy is: choose your access pattern up front, denormalize aggressively, and accept that flexibility is the price of speed.

The three flagship key-value stores occupy different points on the speed/persistence/richness spectrum. **Memcached** (2003, Brad Fitzpatrick, for LiveJournal) is the purest: an in-memory-only cache, no persistence, no replication, no data structures beyond strings, LRU eviction by default. You lose everything on restart — and that's the point. Memcached exists to offload hot reads from the database, nothing more. It's still widely deployed (Facebook, Wikipedia, Twitter) because for pure caching, it's nearly impossible to beat: ~1M ops/sec per instance, ~50 µs latency, dead simple. **Redis** (2009, Salvatore Sanfilippo, originally "REmote DIctionary Server") extended the model with rich data structures — strings, lists, sets, sorted sets (the killer feature for leaderboards), hashes, hyperloglog, streams, geospatial. Redis is single-threaded (mostly), which sounds bad but is brilliant: no locks, no contention, deterministic latency. Redis adds optional persistence (RDB snapshots, AOF append log), replication (async), pub/sub, Lua scripting (atomic server-side operations), and Redis Cluster for sharding. Redis is the most popular key-value store because it's both a cache and a real database — Twitter, GitHub, Stack Overflow, Instagram all run Redis heavily. **Amazon DynamoDB** (2012, based on the 2007 Dynamo paper) is the managed, durable, scaled version: Amazon handles partitioning, replication, HA, backups, and you pay per request. DynamoDB adds a sort key (so within a partition, you can range-query), secondary indexes (local and global), and DynamoDB Streams for CDC. The trade-off is cost at scale and a restrictive query model — but for teams that want "Redis-like access patterns without ops," DynamoDB is unmatched. The choice between them comes down to: do you need persistence and scale (DynamoDB), rich data structures and sub-ms latency (Redis), or pure cache simplicity (Memcached)?

The killer use cases for key-value stores share a common shape: known-key access, low-latency requirement, and tolerance for either staleness (cache) or simple data model (sessions, counters). **Caching** is the canonical use — every major app caches database query results, computed pages, and API responses in Redis/Memcached to absorb 90%+ of read traffic that would otherwise hit the database. Cache-aside is the typical pattern: read cache first, on miss read DB and populate cache, on write invalidate cache. **Session storage** is the second canonical use — web session IDs are random strings (perfect keys), session data is small (a few KB), and reads happen on every request. Storing sessions in Redis (vs. sticky-session tomcats or database-backed sessions) lets you scale stateless web servers freely and survive restarts. **Leaderboards** are Redis's killer app — `ZADD leaderboard 100 alice` adds alice with score 100 to a sorted set, `ZREVRANGE leaderboard 0 9` returns the top 10 in O(log(N)+M) time. Real-world: Reddit, Stack Overflow, and many game backends use Redis sorted sets for their leaderboards. **Rate limiting** is another — `INCR user:42:requests` with `EXPIRE` for a sliding window, atomic server-side. **Real-time bidding** (AdTech) uses Redis for sub-millisecond user-profile lookups during ad auctions. **Counters** (likes, views, downloads) use Redis `INCR` for atomic increments, flushed to the database periodically. **Pub/sub** for chat notifications, **streams** for event logs, **geospatial** (`GEORADIUS`) for "find nearby drivers" — Redis's data structures turn it into a Swiss-army knife for hot-path data.

Real-world deployments illustrate the scale key-value stores reach. **Twitter runs massive Redis clusters** for their timeline, social graph cache, and real-time metrics — billions of ops/sec across the fleet, with custom Redis forks (Twemproxy, later replaced by Cluster) for sharding. Twitter's home timeline is computed by fetching precomputed lists of tweet IDs from Redis (fan-out-on-write), then hydrating the tweets themselves from Redis — sub-50ms p99 for the read path. **Amazon ElastiCache** is the managed Redis/Memcached offering — thousands of AWS customers run it for caching, sessions, and gaming backends, with Amazon handling failover, patching, and backups. ElastiCache for Redis provides read replicas, automatic failover, and multi-AZ — making Redis ops nearly as hands-off as DynamoDB. **Instagram uses Redis** for their feed (sorted sets of post IDs per user), for direct-message inbox, and for rate limiting. **GitHub uses Redis** for their news feed, spam filtering, and rate limiting. **Stack Overflow runs Redis** for caching (their cache hit rate is ~99.9%, meaning 99.9% of page views never touch the database). The pattern is consistent: key-value stores are the hot-path data layer that absorbs the read load and lets the slower durable database (PostgreSQL, MySQL, Cassandra) handle only the writes and the cache misses.

The trade-offs of key-value stores are real and often underestimated. First, **everything must be keyed** — if you can't pre-compute the key, you can't query the data. Want "all sessions created in the last hour"? You need a separate sorted set indexing session IDs by creation time (write-time denormalization). Second, **memory cost** — Redis is RAM-bound; a 5TB dataset requires 5TB of RAM (×3 for replication = 15TB), which is expensive. Memcached is the same. DynamoDB trades RAM-bound for cost-per-request, which can balloon. Third, **persistence is best-effort** — Redis RDB snapshots can lose the last few seconds of writes; AOF mitigates but adds overhead. For critical data, use Redis as a cache alongside a durable store, not as the only copy. Fourth, **eviction policies bite** — when Redis hits `maxmemory`, it evicts by LRU/LFU/random/allkeys-lru. If you accidentally cache too much, hot data may be evicted, causing a thundering herd back to the database. Fifth, **cache stampede** — when a popular cache key expires, hundreds of concurrent requests miss the cache and hammer the database simultaneously. Mitigations: probabilistic early expiration (XFetch), request coalescing, or per-key locks. Sixth, **consistency across instances** — Redis Cluster shards by key, and multi-key operations must be in the same hash slot (Redis hash tags). DynamoDB transactions exist but cost extra. Seventh, **hot keys** — a single key accessed millions of times per second (e.g., a viral tweet) overwhelms the owning shard; mitigations include client-side caching (Redis 6 tracking), key splitting (replicate the hot key N times), and read replicas. The takeaway: key-value stores are simple but not magic — they require careful key design, capacity planning, and cache-invalidation discipline to deliver on their speed promise.

The client issues `GET key` (or `SET`/`DEL`). The KV client hashes the key (`hash(key) % N` where N = shard count) to determine which shard owns it — this is consistent hashing in production (Redis Cluster, DynamoDB), enabling minimal reshuffling when shards change. The request routes directly to the owning shard; in Redis Cluster the client caches the slot map after the first lookup. Each shard is typically a primary + replicas (async replication); writes go to primary, reads can go to replicas (READONLY in Redis Cluster). 2. On the owning shard, the operation is a hash table lookup — O(1) for `GET`/`SET`/`DEL`. Redis is single-threaded for command execution (with I/O threading in newer versions), which means no locks, deterministic latency, and 100k+ ops/sec per instance. Memcached uses worker threads but the same hash-table model. DynamoDB's storage engine uses B-trees for partition-local storage, enabling sort-key range queries within a partition. Sub-millisecond p99 latency is the norm for in-memory KV; DynamoDB adds a few ms for network + replication. 3. The use cases all share the "known key" property: caching (cache key = query hash), sessions (key = session ID), leaderboards (key = "leaderboard:X", value = ZSET of user→score), rate limiting (key = "user:X:window", value = counter + TTL). The bottleneck shifts from query speed to key design and cache invalidation — getting those right is the bulk of KV engineering work. Real-world (Twitter, Instagram, GitHub, Stack Overflow): KV stores absorb 90%+ of read traffic, leaving the durable database to handle only writes and cache misses.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- Key-Value store mock: in-memory LRU cache with TTL, sliding-window rate limiting, atomic INCR (counters), and a sorted-set-style leaderboard.
- In-memory key-value store with LRU + TTL + counters + leaderboard.
- SET key value [EX ttl].
- Atomic INCR.
- If key exists, refresh (move to end = most recently used)
- Evict LRU if at capacity
- Lazy expiry: if TTL passed, evict now
- Mark as recently used

```python
"""
Key-Value store mock: in-memory LRU cache with TTL, sliding-window rate
limiting, atomic INCR (counters), and a sorted-set-style leaderboard.

Demonstrates:
  - O(1) get/set with hash map
  - LRU eviction (when max_capacity hit)
  - TTL-based expiry (lazy + periodic)
  - Atomic INCR for counters
  - Sorted leaderboard (heap-based top-K)
  - Sliding-window rate limiter (INCR + EXPIRE)

Models a simplified Redis-like single-instance KV store.

Run:  python3 kv_store.py
"""

import time
import threading
import heapq
import bisect
from collections import OrderedDict, deque

class KVStore:
    """In-memory key-value store with LRU + TTL + counters + leaderboard."""

    def __init__(self, max_capacity=1000):
        self._data = OrderedDict()              # key -> (value, expiry_ts|None)
        self._lock = threading.RLock()          # reentrant for nested calls
        self.max_capacity = max_capacity
        self._stats = {"hits": 0, "misses": 0, "evictions": 0, "sets": 0}

    # ----- basic ops -----
    def set(self, key, value, ttl_seconds=None):
        """SET key value [EX ttl]. O(1)."""
        with self._lock:
            expiry = time.time() + ttl_seconds if ttl_seconds else None
            # If key exists, refresh (move to end = most recently used)
            if key in self._data:
                self._data.move_to_end(key)
                self._data[key] = (value, expiry)
            else:
                # Evict LRU if at capacity
                while len(self._data) >= self.max_capacity:
                    evicted_key, _ = self._data.popitem(last=False)
                    self._stats["evictions"] += 1
                self._data[key] = (value, expiry)
            self._stats["sets"] += 1

    def get(self, key):
        """GET key. Returns value or None. O(1). Lazily expires."""
        with self._lock:
            if key not in self._data:
                self._stats["misses"] += 1
                return None
            value, expiry = self._data[key]
            # Lazy expiry: if TTL passed, evict now
            if expiry is not None and time.time() > expiry:
                del self._data[key]
                self._stats["misses"] += 1
                return None
            # Mark as recently used
            self._data.move_to_end(key)
            self._stats["hits"] += 1
            return value

    def delete(self, key):
        """DEL key. O(1)."""
        with self._lock:
            return self._data.pop(key, None) is not None

    def exists(self, key):
        """EXISTS key. O(1)."""
        return self.get(key) is not None

    # ----- atomic counters (Redis INCR/DECR) -----
    def incr(self, key, amount=1, ttl_seconds=None):
        """Atomic INCR. Initializes to 0 if absent. Returns new value."""
        with self._lock:
            cur = self.get(key) or 0
            new_val = cur + amount
            self.set(key, new_val, ttl_seconds=ttl_seconds)
            return new_val

    def decr(self, key, amount=1):
        """Atomic DECR."""
        return self.incr(key, -amount)

    # ----- rate limiting (sliding window via counter + TTL) -----
    def rate_limit(self, key, max_requests, window_seconds):
        """
        Returns True if request allowed, False if rate-limited.
        Pattern: INCR key, set TTL on first request, check count.
        """
        with self._lock:
            count = self.incr(key, ttl_seconds=window_seconds)
            return count <= max_requests, count

    # ----- leaderboard (Redis ZSET simplified) -----
    def leaderboard_add(self, key, member, score):
        """ZADD key score member. Stores sorted by score."""
        lb_key = f"__lb__:{key}"
        with self._lock:
            lb = self.get(lb_key) or {}  # member -> score
            lb[member] = score
            self.set(lb_key, lb)
            return len(lb)

    def leaderboard_top(self, key, count=10):
        """ZREVRANGE key 0 count-1 WITHSCORES. Top N by score desc."""
        lb_key = f"__lb__:{key}"
        with self._lock:
            lb = self.get(lb_key) or {}
            # Sort by score descending, take top N
            sorted_items = sorted(lb.items(), key=lambda x: -x[1])
            return sorted_items[:count]

    def leaderboard_rank(self, key, member):
        """ZRANK key member. Returns 0-indexed rank or None."""
        lb_key = f"__lb__:{key}"
        with self._lock:
            lb = self.get(lb_key) or {}
            if member not in lb:
                return None
            sorted_items = sorted(lb.items(), key=lambda x: -x[1])
            for i, (m, _) in enumerate(sorted_items):
                if m == member:
                    return i
            return None

    # ----- maintenance & stats -----
    def evict_expired(self):
        """Periodic expiry sweep. Walk all keys, drop expired."""
        with self._lock:
            now = time.time()
            expired = []
            for k, (_, exp) in self._data.items():
                if exp is not None and now > exp:
                    expired.append(k)
            for k in expired:
                del self._data[k]
            return len(expired)

    def stats(self):
        with self._lock:
            total = self._stats["hits"] + self._stats["misses"]
            hit_rate = self._stats["hits"] / total if total else 0
            return {
                **self._stats,
                "size": len(self._data),
                "hit_rate": f"{hit_rate:.1%}",
            }

# ---------- Demo ----------
if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("=== Key-Value Store demo (LRU + TTL + counters + leaderboard) ===\n")
    kv = KVStore(max_capacity=5)

    print("--- Basic ops: SET / GET / DEL ---")
    kv.set("user:1", {"name": "alice", "email": "a@x.com"})
    kv.set("user:2", {"name": "bob"})
    print(f"  GET user:1 = {kv.get('user:1')}")
    print(f"  GET user:2 = {kv.get('user:2')}")
    print(f"  GET user:3 (missing) = {kv.get('user:3')}")
    print(f"  EXISTS user:2 = {kv.exists('user:2')}")
    print(f"  DEL user:2 = {kv.delete('user:2')}")
    print(f"  EXISTS user:2 = {kv.exists('user:2')}")

    print("\n--- TTL: key expires after 0.2s ---")
    kv.set("temp:1", "ephemeral", ttl_seconds=0.2)
    print(f"  GET immediately = {kv.get('temp:1')}")
    time.sleep(0.25)
    print(f"  GET after 0.25s = {kv.get('temp:1')} (expired)")

    print("\n--- LRU eviction (capacity=5) ---")
    for i in range(7):
        kv.set(f"k{i}", i)  # forces eviction of k0, k1
    print(f"  GET k0 (evicted) = {kv.get('k0')}")
    print(f"  GET k6 (present) = {kv.get('k6')}")
    print(f"  Stats: {kv.stats()}")

    print("\n--- Atomic INCR (counters: likes, views) ---")
    for _ in range(100):
        kv.incr("post:42:likes")
    print(f"  post:42:likes after 100x INCR = {kv.get('post:42:likes')}")
    kv.incr("post:42:likes", amount=5)  # INCRBY
    print(f"  after INCRBY 5 = {kv.get('post:42:likes')}")

    print("\n--- Sliding-window rate limiter (100 req / 1s) ---")
    allowed = 0
    blocked = 0
    for _ in range(150):
        ok, count = kv.rate_limit("user:1:rl", max_requests=100,
                                  window_seconds=1)
        if ok:
            allowed += 1
        else:
            blocked += 1
    print(f"  Attempted 150 requests: {allowed} allowed, {blocked} blocked")

    print("\n--- Leaderboard (Redis ZSET style) ---")
    lb = KVStore()
    scores = [("alice", 100), ("bob", 95), ("carol", 88),
              ("dave", 110), ("eve", 75), ("frank", 105)]
    for member, score in scores:
        lb.leaderboard_add("game:1", member, score)
    print(f"  Top 3: {lb.leaderboard_top('game:1', 3)}")
    print(f"  alice rank: {lb.leaderboard_rank('game:1', 'alice')}")
    print(f"  dave rank:  {lb.leaderboard_rank('game:1', 'dave')}")

    print("\n--- Cache-aside pattern (cache miss -> DB -> populate) ---")
    db = {"product:1": {"name": "Widget", "price": 9.99}}
    cache = KVStore()

    def get_product(pid):
        # 1. Try cache
        val = cache.get(f"product:{pid}")
        if val is not None:
            print(f"  [CACHE HIT]  product:{pid} = {val}")
            return val
        # 2. Cache miss -> read DB
        print(f"  [CACHE MISS] reading DB for product:{pid}")
        val = db.get(f"product:{pid}")
        if val is not None:
            cache.set(f"product:{pid}", val, ttl_seconds=60)
        return val

    get_product(1)  # miss, populates cache
    get_product(1)  # hit
    get_product(1)  # hit

    print(f"\n=== Final stats ===\n  {kv.stats()}")
    print(f"  {lb.stats()}")
    print(f"  {cache.stats()}")
    print("\n  Key-value trade-offs:")
    print("    + O(1) get/put, sub-ms latency, simple to scale (hash key)")
    print("    + Redis data structures enable leaderboards, rate limit, etc.")
    print("    - everything must be keyed; no ad-hoc queries")
    print("    - RAM-bound (cost); persistence is best-effort")
    print("    - cache invalidation + stampede + hot keys are real problems")
```

Hot keys are a classic Redis scaling problem — a single key on one shard gets disproportionate traffic, capping throughput at that shard's limit (~100k ops/sec).
A Redis sorted set (ZSET) is a set where each member has an associated floating-point score, and the set is sorted by score.
A key-value store is O(1) because it's literally a hash map — the key is hashed (e.g., MurmurHash3 in Redis, MD5 in Memcached), and the hash determines the bucket/slot…
quiz.explanation: A key-value store is O(1) because it's literally a hash map — the key is hashed (e.g., MurmurHash3 in Redis, MD5 in Memcached), and the hash determines the bucket/slot in memory (or the shard in a distributed system). Hash map lookups are constant time regardless of dataset size. The implication for query flexibility is severe: you can ONLY query by exact key.

quiz.explanation: A Redis sorted set (ZSET) is a set where each member has an associated floating-point score, and the set is sorted by score. Operations: ZADD key score member adds/updates, ZREVRANGE key 0 9 returns top 10 by score (highest first), ZRANK key member returns the 0-indexed rank, ZSCORE key member returns the score, ZINCRBY key delta member atomically increments a member's score.
